artworks.title: Exploring Old Ironsides: New Perspectives
artworks.description: Large photographs by Greg M. Cooper, who has photographed USS Constitution for the museum for more than 20 years: the ship underway in Boston Harbor, close details in dry dock, hidden interiors and passing weather. It opened the museum’s re-envisioned Special Exhibition Gallery, with daylight and the exposed structure of the old Navy Yard pump house. Presented by the Yawkey Foundation.
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibition Gallery: the renewed gallery for changing shows, with daylight and the old pump house’s structure
artworks.placeNote: Which gallery the show is in is a guess (the museum’s map of 2024 calls this room Today’s Navy).

artworks.title: Art of the Ship
artworks.description: In the museum’s theater: artwork of “Old Ironsides” from the museum’s collection, from dramatic scenes of life at sea to how artists have imagined, remembered and celebrated America’s Ship of State. Supported by The Boston Marine Society.
artworks.galleryName: Theater: Art of the Ship (and the museum’s films)

artworks.title: “Old Ironsides” in War and Peace
artworks.description: Three centuries of USS Constitution: her building in Boston and the early U.S. Navy, the highs and lows of the War of 1812, diplomatic voyages and her preservation, and how she became a national icon (look for the head of the Andrew Jackson figurehead, sawn off the ship one night in 1834). You can touch different woods, build a ship from puzzle pieces and see a model taller than you.
artworks.galleryName: “Old Ironsides” in War and Peace: the long hall, from the ship’s building to the War of 1812

artworks.title: The battle room
artworks.description: A room about the experience of battle in the War of 1812, with two cannons that roar when all their buttons are pushed in order (it is loud: the hall next door is quieter).
artworks.galleryName: “Old Ironsides” in War and Peace: battle, diplomatic voyages and preservation, with the cannon room

artworks.title: The Model Shop
artworks.description: Volunteer model makers at work on miniature ships; when nobody is at the bench you can see finished models through the windows. The Guild also holds the yearly Masters of Miniature ship model show.
artworks.galleryName: Model Shop of the USS Constitution Model Shipwright Guild (windows onto the bench)

artworks.title: All Hands on Deck: A Sailor’s Life in 1812
artworks.description: Join Constitution’s 1812 crew: meet real sailors and their families back home (found in decades of research in census records, diaries, letters and pension files), then scrub the deck, lie in a hammock, fire a cannon as a team and go aloft to furl a sail.
artworks.galleryName: All Hands on Deck: A Sailor’s Life in 1812 (hands-on: scrub the deck, swing in a hammock, furl a sail)

artworks.title: Battle Theater
artworks.description: A short captioned film inside All Hands on Deck that tells the story of one of Constitution’s famous battles of the War of 1812.
artworks.galleryName: Battle Theater: the film of a famous battle of 1812

artworks.title: USS Constitution, “Old Ironsides”
artworks.artist: Joshua Humphreys (design); built at Edmund Hartt’s shipyard, Boston
artworks.medium: 44-gun frigate: live oak, white oak, pine
artworks.description: The world’s oldest commissioned warship still afloat, crewed by active-duty U.S. Navy sailors who lead the tours. She never lost a battle; her nickname comes from 1812, when British cannonballs seemed to bounce off her thick oak sides in the fight with HMS Guerriere. Free to board (Navy security screening; photo ID for 18 and over).
artworks.galleryName: Spar deck (the top deck), amidships: the mainmast, the carronades and the hatch down to the gun deck

artworks.title: The double wheel
artworks.description: Constitution is steered from a double wheel on the quarterdeck, so up to four sailors could hold her in a blow. Her wheel was shot away in the battle with HMS Java on December 29, 1812; the museum tells the story of the wheels that came after.
artworks.galleryName: Quarterdeck: the double wheel, the mizzenmast and the officers’ deck

artworks.title: The carronades
artworks.description: The short, heavy guns along the top deck are carronades, which threw a 32-pound ball at close range. Like every gun on board today they are 20th-century replicas.
artworks.galleryName: Spar deck (the top deck), amidships: the mainmast, the carronades and the hatch down to the gun deck

artworks.title: Masts and rigging
artworks.description: Three masts (fore, main and mizzen) and miles of rigging carry nearly an acre of sail when she is fully rigged. The mainmast stands about 220 feet above the waterline.
artworks.galleryName: Forecastle at the bow: the foremast, the bell and the anchors

artworks.title: The gun deck battery
artworks.description: Her main battery: thirty 24-pounder long guns, fifteen on each side, each worked by a crew of about a dozen men. The guns on board today are replicas; two can fire salutes.
artworks.galleryName: Gun deck: thirty 24-pounder long guns, fifteen a side, the capstan and the pumps
artworks.placeNote: One deck below the top deck: down the steep ladder.
artworks.imageCredit: Naval History & Heritage Command Detachment Boston, via the USS Constitution Museum

artworks.title: The captain’s cabin
artworks.description: The captain lived, worked and dined at the stern of the gun deck, in a great cabin lit by the stern windows, with his dining cabin and sleeping cabins beside it. Visitors look in from the door; in battle the bulkheads came down and guns stood here too.
artworks.galleryName: Captain’s cabin at the stern: the great cabin, the dining cabin and the sleeping cabins (seen from the door)
artworks.placeNote: At the stern of the gun deck.

artworks.title: The galley stove
artworks.description: All the crew’s food was cooked on one big iron stove forward on the gun deck: salt beef and pork, peas, biscuit and burgoo for some 450 people.
artworks.galleryName: Galley stove and the bow (the manger)

artworks.title: Hammocks on the berth deck
artworks.description: The crew slept on the berth deck in hammocks slung from the beams, about 14 inches apart, and kept their few belongings in sea bags and chests. The enormous white oak knees that hold the hull together are here too.
artworks.galleryName: Berth deck: where some 450 sailors slung their hammocks
artworks.placeNote: Two decks down; on the guided tour, sometimes closed.
artworks.imageCredit: Naval History & Heritage Command Detachment Boston, via the USS Constitution Museum

artworks.title: The wardroom
artworks.description: The officers ate and spent their free time in the wardroom at the stern of the berth deck, with small staterooms on each side.
artworks.placeNote: Two decks down, at the stern; on the guided tour, sometimes closed.

artworks.title: USS Cassin Young (DD-793)
artworks.description: A World War II destroyer, hit twice by kamikazes off Okinawa in 1945, moored on the other side of Pier 1 and shown by the National Park Service (check the Park Service for days and hours).
artworks.galleryName: USS Cassin Young (DD-793), a World War II destroyer run by the National Park Service

artworks.title: Charlestown Navy Yard Visitor Center
artworks.description: The Park Service’s visitor center in Building 5: rangers, exhibits on the Navy Yard’s 174 years, restrooms, and the way to Pier 1.
artworks.galleryName: Charlestown Navy Yard Visitor Center (National Park Service, Building 5): rangers, exhibits, restrooms
